slides: Okay, a quick summary before the mixed fraction practice.
Every rule from the fraction lessons... in about three minutes.
Think of it like this. More cakes, everyone gets more. More people, everyone gets less.
Improper to mixed: how many times it fits, and the remainder goes on top.
Mixed to improper: whole times denominator, plus numerator. Same denominator.
And a denominator can never be zero.
Expand or reduce: the same factor on top and bottom. The value stays.
Cancel factors only. Never a term in a sum.
Now, one minus sign can sit anywhere. Two minus signs cancel.
Top times top, bottom times bottom. Cancel first, and the numbers stay small.
And "of the rest" means of what's left. Not of the whole.
Multiply by the reciprocal. And flip only the second one.
Mixed numbers first become improper fractions. Never multiply the parts separately.
So you count how many tenths fit into two fifths... four.
Adding and subtracting need a common denominator. So run through the multiples of the bigger one: nine, no. Eighteen, yes.
Then add the tops. The denominator stays.
A whole number can wear any denominator. And mixed numbers? Improper fractions first.
Same order as Topic 1: multiply and divide before add and subtract.
Work out the whole top and the whole bottom first. Then divide.
So, name the operation. Then use its rule.
Six sevenths is almost one. Five ninths is a little more than a half. So the sum is about one and a half.
One example that fails kills a rule.
Cross shortcut: multiply across and add on top, multiply the bottoms. Now, these are for speed... the safe method always works.
Decimal places tell you the zeros in the denominator.
And to compare decimals, give them the same number of places. So zero point five nine is bigger than zero point five one two.
Okay, before you practice, ask yourself these questions.
Adding needs a common denominator. Multiplying doesn't.
The traps: adding tops and bottoms, flipping the wrong fraction, splitting the bottom, and "of the rest."
Good luck.
